titre: Siccar Point, 1788: A Test, Not a Revelation
accroche: The story goes that Hutton grasped the age of the Earth there in June 1788. His theory was already written: the boat trip put it to the test.
contenu_vulgarise:
June 1788, fine weather. A boat leaves Dunglass Burn, on Scotland's east coast. On board are three men: the geologist James Hutton, the mathematician John Playfair, and Sir James Hall, 27, the young baronet of Dunglass. The usual account turns this into a scene of illumination: Hutton lands at Siccar Point and suddenly understands that the Earth is immensely old. It's a lovely story. It's also backward.

## What the Three Men See

On the headland, layers of gray sandstone stand almost vertical. Above them, red sandstones lie almost flat. The first date from the early Silurian, the second from the late Devonian, and several tens of millions of years separate them, according to NASA. Their contact, laid bare by the sea, is called an angular unconformity.

Hutton reads in it a sequence of events. The first set was deposited on the floor of a sea, then folded, uplifted, and eroded. A second set then covered it, and the whole was in turn uplifted and tilted. In his own description of the place, he notes a modest detail: most of the fragments of older rock caught in the red sandstone have sharp angles. They therefore did not travel far, nor were they worn down by abrasion. Playfair, for his part, left the line that made the site's reputation: his mind grew giddy looking so far into the abyss of time.

## An Idea Already There

Three years earlier, in 1785, Hutton had set out his ideas before the Royal Society of Edinburgh. The 1785 abstract specified that, as far as human observation goes, the world has neither a beginning nor an end. His critics did not heed that qualification and accused him of upholding an eternal Earth. Since then, he had visited two other unconformities in Scotland, less striking ones. Siccar Point, moreover, is not the first unconformity ever described: according to Kerr, French texts on the Alps already mentioned them, and Hutton had alluded to them.

The most famous sentence, the one that closes the 1788 text of the *Theory of the Earth*, says that one finds neither a vestige of a beginning nor a prospect of an end. It is sometimes said to have been born on that headland. According to the geologist Andrew Kerr, that is unlikely: the text was already finished and does not mention the outing. The headland was the testing ground of a concept, not its origin.

## What the Story Shifts

A revelation by the water's edge makes a better story than a method. Yet it was the method that took place: an idea formed in advance, then a place where it could fail and did not. How many discovery legends are in fact verifications told as revelations?

repere.texte: According to the geologist Andrew Kerr (2018), the June 1788 excursion took place three years after the 1785 presentation of Hutton's theory; the 1788 text of the Theory of the Earth was already finished and does not mention the outing. Siccar Point served to test a concept, not to spark it.
repere.source: Andrew Kerr, “Hutton's Unconformity at Siccar Point, Scotland,” Geoscience Canada, 45(1), 2018

carte.punch: Siccar Point: Hutton came to test a three-year-old theory, not to discover it.
carte.idee: In June 1788, Hutton, Playfair, and Hall sail along the Scottish coast. The theory of deep time had been presented since 1785, and the 1788 text does not mention the outing: according to Kerr, the headland tested a concept; it did not give birth to it.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Hutton, “Theory of the Earth,” Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, vol. 1 (1788)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The 1788 text that Kerr points out was finished before the boat trip.

quiz.question: According to the geologist Andrew Kerr, what role did the 1788 excursion to Siccar Point play in Hutton's thinking?
choix: It suddenly revealed to him that the Earth was far older than 6,000 years
It tested an idea formed before it, through a striking example
It showed him what an unconformity is, something never described before him
It inspired the final sentence of his theory, written on the headland itself
quiz.explication: Hutton had already presented his theory in 1785, which challenged the 6,000-year age accepted by almost everyone at the time: the excursion did not reveal it to him. He had also visited two other Scottish unconformities, and texts on the Alps already described some: this was not the first. Finally, according to Kerr, the 1788 text was finished and does not mention the outing: the headland served as a test, not as an origin.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who wrote that his mind grew giddy looking so far into the abyss of time, at Siccar Point?
choix: James Hutton
Sir James Hall
John Playfair
Andrew Kerr
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It was Playfair, the group's mathematician, who left this line that became the site's reputation; Hutton himself did not write it in his 1788 text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What detail does Hutton note about the fragments of older rock caught in the red sandstone?
choix: Their angles are sharp, a sign they did not travel far
They are rounded by long transport
They contain intact marine fossils
They are the same color as the gray sandstone
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says most of the fragments have sharp angles, proof that they neither traveled far nor were worn down by abrasion, unlike the other three options, which it does not mention.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Before Siccar Point, had Hutton already seen this kind of contact between two sets of rocks?
choix: No, Siccar Point is the very first unconformity he observes
No, he only knows the phenomenon from texts on the Alps
Yes, but only from other geologists' accounts
Yes, he had already visited two other unconformities in Scotland, less striking ones
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that he had since visited two other unconformities in Scotland, less striking ones, and that Siccar Point is not the first one described elsewhere either, since French texts on the Alps already mentioned them.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to NASA, how much time separates the deposition of the Silurian gray sandstones from that of the Devonian red sandstones at Siccar Point?
choix: A few hundred thousand years
Several tens of millions of years
About a billion years
Less than a million years
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text cites NASA for putting the gap between the two sets at several tens of millions of years, far more than the other options offered.
